name: Handshake
summary: Handshake operates a career network and recruiting platform focused on students and early-career talent, connecting employers with a large university-based candidate base.
overview: Handshake is a career network for students and recent graduates that sells recruiting access and workflow tools to employers. In January 2022, it announced a $200 million Series F at a $3.5 billion valuation, a benchmark that has not been superseded by a disclosed priced round in this profile.

facts.label: Latest financing
facts.note: Handshake raised $200 million in a Series F at a $3.5 billion valuation.

bull_case: University distribution and employer relationships can create an enduring network effect in the early-career hiring market.
bear_case: Hiring budgets are cyclical, while AI-enabled recruiting tools and incumbent job platforms compete for the same employer spend.
latest_round: January 2022 Series F: $200M at a $3.5B valuation
directory_notes: Public financing and operating data remain limited.

intelligence.description: A career network connecting students and early-career candidates with employers.
company: Handshake gives employers a channel to recruit university students and recent graduates, while candidates use the platform to find career opportunities. Its January 2022 Series F was led by existing and new investors at a $3.5 billion valuation.

The company is exposed to the structure of graduate hiring, which can be sensitive to macro hiring conditions. Its installed university relationships are valuable, but a new valuation or updated operating disclosure has not been announced in this profile.
intelligence.why_it_matters: Early-career recruiting is a large, fragmented workflow category where network density matters. Handshake offers a private-company perspective on how AI and hiring-market shifts are changing talent acquisition.

changed.text: Handshake announced a $200M Series F at a $3.5B valuation.

takeaways: Handshake's disclosed valuation benchmark is the January 2022 Series F.
University and employer participation underpin its network model.
Hiring cycles and competition in recruiting software remain central risks.
